Figure 9 illustrates how context-length compatibility can change the routing decision when KV affinity is inconclusive. Figure 9 : Illustrative example comparing routing decisions. When KV affinity is inconclusive, reuse- and load-aware routing selects the minimum-load GPU, while Coda selects a load-safe GPU whose active contexts better match the arriving 48K request. Dynamic reevaluation. Coda refreshes local KV reuse, worker load, and active context composition at every routing opportunity. These measurements reflect only the current system state and do not rely on predicted output lengths or future tool-return times. When context telemetry is unavailable or no load-eligible worker has an active decode population, Coda retains the reuse- and load-aware destination. Routing changes only the arriving request’s assignment and does not migrate requests that are already GPU-active. Once assigned, the request enters the selected worker’s admission layer (§ 4 ) for KV-state preparation and model execution. 6 Implementation Runtime integration. We implement Coda as an orchestration layer with approximately 2.9 KLoC of core policy and planning code, connected to the inference backend through an adapter. The adapter adds hooks to request dispatch, waiting-queue selection, and model execution. At each hook, Coda reads the current runtime state and returns a routing, state-admission, or execution-admission decision. The backend continues to handle memory allocation, KV-state movement, preemption, model execution, and sampling. Routing and admission paths. The dispatcher maintains asynchronously refreshed worker snapshots and uses a consistent snapshot version for each arriving request. The resulting routing decision is attached to the request before normal dispatch. At each state-admission opportunity, Coda examines a bounded frontier of at most 64 candidate entries and queries the KV manager for reusable-prefix matches, KV-block demand, and usable HBM capacity. Candidate inspection is read-only, and the selected entry is promoted through one remove-and-prepend operation before native scheduling continues. For an accepted execution plan, Coda reorders the persistent batch through state-safe row swaps and constructs cohort-specific views of the required attention metadata. Each model layer performs one complete-population KV update, invokes the existing attention operator once for each context-compatible cohort, and writes each cohort’s results into the corresponding region of the original output buffer. Dense or MoE computation and sampling remain unchanged. Figure 10 : Illustrative example of CPU-shadow offloading. A completed KV-state chunk is asynchronously published from GPU HBM to the CPU shadow. Under HBM pressure, the GPU copy can be reclaimed without an eviction-time transfer, while the CPU copy remains available for subsequent restoration and reuse. CPU-shadow offloading and HBM reclaim. The KV connector asynchronously publishes completed KV-state chunks to a shared CPU shadow in DRAM and restores matching KV-state chunks on demand. Once publication completes, the corresponding HBM copy can be reclaimed without an eviction-time GPU-to-CPU transfer. Figure 10 illustrates CPU-shadow publication, HBM reclaim, and on-demand restoration. When decode execution requires additional HBM blocks, the backend automatically invokes HBM reclaim. Following CacheWise’s cache-reclaim integration [ 21 ] , Coda determines the HBM reclaim victims using a tool-call-aware policy. Within a bounded victim window, it prioritizes valid, uniquely owned KV states predicted to remain inactive longer based on tool-call identity and elapsed tool-call time.
